data.title: Manufacturing output growth accelerates in October
data.description:
Precision engineering led the gains, jumping 54.1%, whilst biomedical fell 35.8%.

Singapore’s manufacturing output expanded 6.1% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.4% growth in September, according to the Economic Development Board.

Excluding biomedical manufacturing, output increased 12%, up from 9% in the previous month.

All manufacturing clusters, except transport engineering and biomedical manufacturing, recorded output growth.

Precision engineering led the gains, rising 54.1% on the back of higher semiconductor equipment production in the machinery and systems segment.

Electronics grew 6.6%, with all segments expanding amidst sustained artificial intelligence-related demand.

Chemicals grew 4.4%, with higher output of fragrances in the other chemicals segment and increased production of industrial gases, chemicals, and food additives in the specialties segment.

The petroleum segment also recorded higher production of refined products, whilst the petrochemicals segment declined amidst softer demand and feedstock supply disruptions.

General manufacturing industries grew 0.5%, supported by higher production of milk powder and beverage products in the food, beverages, and tobacco segment.

In contrast, the miscellaneous and printing segments recorded output declines, with the former reflecting lower production of structural metal products and furniture.

Transport engineering declined 5.3% due to lower shipyard activities and weak production of oil and gas field equipment, whilst the land and aerospace segments expanded, with the latter supported by higher production of aircraft parts and engine maintenance, repair, and overhaul.

Biomedical manufacturing declined 35.8% due to lower production of biologics and a change in mix of active pharmaceutical ingredients in the pharmaceuticals segment.

data.title: MPA explores ethanol and biomethane bunkering trials with CMA CGM
data.description:
Singapore will assess biomethane's emissions savings under different frameworks.

The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) is exploring ethanol and liquefied biomethane bunkering trials with France-based CMA CGM as it advances efforts to develop lower-emission marine fuels and strengthen the country's bunkering capabilities.

MPA and CMA CGM are exploring a near-term liquefied biomethane bunkering trial with industry partners.

The trial will examine how to account for and recognise the fuel's sustainability benefits and greenhouse gas emissions savings under different regulatory and voluntary frameworks, MPA said in a statement on 26 November.

CMA CGM is separately evaluating prospective ethanol bunkering trials to assess the fuel's use in marine engines, alongside associated bunkering procedures, safety considerations, and operational requirements.

The development of liquefied biomethane supply pathways builds on Singapore's established liquefied natural gas (LNG) bunkering capabilities. CMA CGM already regularly undertakes LNG bunkering in the city-state.

MPA and CMA CGM have also conducted digital data-exchange trials involving APL SINGAPURA in 2025 and CMA CGM GRAND PALAIS in 2026.

The tests examined how digital exchanges could simplify port clearance, reduce manual processes, and improve port-call efficiency.

Their findings will support a pilot in the first quarter of 2027 and contribute to strengthening digital connectivity between ships and ports.

The initiatives build on a broader partnership between MPA and CMA CGM, formalised through a memorandum of understanding (MOU) renewed in March 2025, which focuses on maritime decarbonisation, digitalisation, and innovation.

On innovation, CMA CGM Group's accelerator ZEBOX and PIER71 signed a partnership agreement on 18 November to strengthen cooperation between their maritime innovation ecosystems.

The agreement will facilitate exchanges between startups, improve access to new markets and connect entrepreneurs with industry partners.

CMA CGM and the Singapore Maritime Foundation also signed a separate MOU on 25 November to support MaritimeONE scholarships and internships for the next generation of maritime professionals.

Since 2019, CMA CGM has supported 11 students through MPA's Global Internship Award, providing internships at its Singapore offices and overseas rotations in France, China, Australia, Malaysia, Taiwan, and the Philippines.

The placements covered operations, trade management, sales, and marketing.

MPA and CMA CGM are also looking at a collaboration on the Maritime Leadership Programme in 2027 to develop the next generation of maritime leaders in Singapore.

Meanwhile, CMA CGM's intra-Asia shipping specialist CNC introduced new services and enhanced existing connections in 2026, linking Singapore with markets including Malaysia, Indonesia, and Myanmar.

These developments further support the city-state's position as an international maritime hub.

“These initiatives bring together our respective capabilities to address the evolving needs of international shipping,” said MPA Chief Executive Ang Wee Keong.

data.title: Maybank raises 2027 GDP forecast to 4.2% on AI capex
data.description:
However, the bank says domestic conditions are likely to stay subdued.

Maybank revised up its 2027 GDP growth forecast for Singapore to 4.2% from 3.3%, as the artificial intelligence (AI) capital expenditure cycle will likely remain strong in the first half of 2027.

The figure is at the upper end of the Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry's forecast of 2.5% to 4.5%.

Maybank said economic growth should remain solid in 2027, even as the exceptional AI boom seen in 2026 is likely to moderate.

Strong global demand for AI compute should support electronic exports and investment, but hyperscaler capex growth will likely slow from this year's exceptional pace.

Singapore will also continue to benefit from semiconductor capacity expansion, including the ramp-up of Micron's high-bandwidth memory advanced-packaging facility and VisionPower Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s 300-millimetre wafer fab.

The megaproject construction pipeline and investments in energy infrastructure under the Energy Market Authority's five-year plan should also support growth.

Meanwhile, domestic conditions are likely to remain more subdued, reinforcing a K-shaped expansion, the bank said.

The "low-hire, low-quit" labour market, rising retrenchments, and slower wage growth could keep households cautious and dampen consumer-facing sectors, even as export-oriented industries and fixed investment remain robust.

There could also be more cross-border competition and increased outbound travel with the Johor-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link opening from February 2027.

Maybank expects the US Federal Reserve to tighten by an additional 25 basis points in December 2026 and another 25 in 2027.

It also expects the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) to maintain the current pace of appreciation of the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate for the rest of 2026 and in 2027.

The country's GDP growth eased slightly to 6.1% year-on-year in the third quarter (Q3) of 2026, from 6.4% in the previous quarter. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the economy grew 1.5%.

Strong AI-related demand drove the growth, supported by wholesale trade, electronics, precision engineering, and robust loan demand.

MAS estimated that tech-related sectors accounted for 75% of overall GDP growth in Q3.

data.title: Tokenisation loosens treasurers’ yield-liquidity trade-off
data.description:
Standard Chartered sees CBDCs as the base, tokenised deposits as scale, and stablecoins as reach.

Corporate treasurers are looking to digital assets to put excess cash to work without losing rapid access to liquidity when funds are needed.

In an interview at the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF 2026) last November 18-20, Ying Ying Tan, Global Head of Securities Services and Global Head of Digital Assets at Standard Chartered, said tokenisation can improve settlement speed, availability, and on-chain finality.

That is particularly relevant for treasury teams managing cash across multiple banks, currencies and jurisdictions, where fragmented infrastructure can make liquidity harder to mobilise efficiently.

Tan said digital assets can allow companies to move excess liquidity into instruments offering better returns and convert those funds back into conventional money almost in real time when required.

“[They] are able to move their excess liquidity into instruments that can have a better returns than what the conventional world provides,” Tan said. That gives treasurers more room to improve yield without tying up cash they may need to redeploy quickly.

The next question is how different forms of digital money fit into institutional settlement. Tan does not expect central bank digital currencies, tokenised deposits or regulated stablecoins to dominate on their own. Instead, she sees each serving a different function.

CBDCs would provide the foundation for money clearing, whilst tokenised deposits would support scale in money movement across institutions.

Stablecoins, meanwhile, could extend reach into smaller economies and markets where broader access is needed.

“CBDC or central bank money provides the foundation, tokenised deposits provide the scale, and stable coins will provide the outreach,” Tan said.

For treasurers, the commercial issue is therefore less about choosing a single digital rail and more about how effectively these instruments can work together to improve returns whilst keeping liquidity available on demand.

data.title: Digital trade pact lowers compliance risk for fintechs
data.description:
Italy sees SME-heavy markets creating similar fintech needs across Europe and Southeast Asia.

The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement is giving fintech companies a clearer framework to test cross-border business models without running into conflicting data and regulatory requirements.

In an interview during the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF 2026), Dante Brandi, Ambassador of Italy to Singapore and Brunei Darussalam at the Embassy of Italy in Singapore, said the agreement can help technology and financial services move between Singapore and the European Union.

“For the Italian startups in the fintech festival, having this legal framework is crucial because it provides a legal ecosystem where data models can be tested,” Brandi said.

He said companies can use the framework to develop models that comply with regulations in both markets before pursuing wider regional expansion.

That reduces one of the main barriers facing fintechs seeking to scale internationally: having to adapt products and data practices to different legal environments.

Brandi said the opportunity also runs in the opposite direction, with Italy providing a potential European entry point for Asian fintech companies. He pointed to similarities between Italy and Southeast Asia, particularly their large populations of small and medium-sized enterprises and family-owned businesses.

“The technology solutions provided by Italian fintech, insurtech companies are very much aligned with the needs of both ecosystems of SMEs and family businesses,” he said.

For fintech companies, that overlap means products designed around the needs of SMEs and family businesses in one market may also address similar problems in the other, strengthening the commercial case for cross-border expansion.

Italy’s financial system remains heavily reliant on banks, which Brandi said creates demand for technology supporting families and smaller companies. That includes solutions addressing scams, cross-border payments and overseas transactions.

As an exporting economy, Italy also creates demand for tools that help SMEs reach foreign customers, receive payments and manage international business.

The broader opportunity is to turn common digital rules into a practical corridor for fintechs seeking to expand between Europe and Southeast Asia.

data.title: MUFG prioritises safety as it expands AI adoption
data.description:
The bank is adapting deployment across 17 Asia-Pacific markets as regulation and client risk tolerance vary.

MUFG Bank is expanding its use of artificial intelligence across Asia-Pacific while prioritising accuracy, client requirements and risk controls over speed of deployment.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF 2026), Osamu Abe, Chief of Staff for Asia-Pacific at MUFG Bank, said the lender is prepared to adjust the pace of adoption where necessary rather than compromise on safety.

“I would rather say we value safety and accuracy over the sheer speed,” Abe said.

He said this after mentioning that AI can take on more technical banking work such as financial modelling and analysis, but human judgement remains critical when that analysis feeds into major transactions.

Abe pointed to project finance and mergers and acquisitions, where decisions can affect businesses and communities for years.

For MUFG, the harder task is therefore not improving AI’s technical capability but applying its output to transactions where market conditions, client relationships, and long-term consequences still require human judgement.

Over the next 24 months, Abe expects AI systems to become more technically accurate, shifting the challenge towards how banks apply them in real-world dealmaking.

That becomes more complicated across MUFG’s 17 Asia-Pacific markets, where regulation, business practices, culture, and client risk tolerance differ. The bank also holds stakes in partner banks in Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam.

Abe said the bank is willing to deploy more AI and tolerate some mistakes during the earlier stages of adoption, but those errors must not affect clients in the wrong way.

“We are making sure we adjust to each client set, and we deploy our long-term relationships and knowledge of our clients when we do that to adjust our AI,” he said.

The bank is therefore treating AI adoption as a market-by-market exercise rather than a uniform regional rollout.

The approach points to a market-by-market rollout rather than a uniform regional model, allowing MUFG to scale AI while preserving human judgement and local client knowledge.

data.title: Banks rethink fraud controls as authenticated scams rise
data.description:
Visa says behavioural and network signals can expose coercion missed by transaction checks.

Banks need to look beyond transaction authentication as scams increasingly manipulate customers into approving payments themselves, according to Visa.

Speaking on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival (SFF 2026), held from Nov. 18 to 20 at Singapore EXPO, Serene Gay, Asia Pacific Head of Visa Value-Added Services, said an authenticated transaction may not reflect a customer’s actual intent.

“The scariest thing that we need to look out for today is that whilst the transaction is being authenticated, it may not necessarily reflect the intention and the state of mind that the consumer is in,” Gay said.

She said behavioural intelligence can help banks detect deviations from how customers normally interact with mobile devices and banking applications, including finger strokes, password entry timing, and tapping behaviour.

These signals can help identify cases where a transaction appears legitimate but the customer may be acting under manipulation or coercion.

Gay said banks should also combine know-your-customer and transaction data with broader network-level intelligence to identify fraud patterns across banks, merchants, countries and regions.

She added that another weakness is fragmentation between cybersecurity and payment fraud teams. Financial institutions now need a unified view of the customer journey rather than treating cyber threats and payment signals separately, Gay said.

“Many times, it's not about knowing, but it's about how quickly they are able to prioritise and respond to the important ones,” she said.

Gay said combining cybersecurity signals with downstream payment fraud information can help banks prioritise threats earlier.

She added that network-level transaction trends can reveal fraud patterns that may not be visible within a single bank.

The broader challenge is for banks to detect manipulation even when the payment itself has already passed authentication.

data.title: BFA Global Investors sets up Asia HQ in Singapore
data.description:
Local investors can now connect with US opportunities.

BFA Global Investors, a US private investment manager, established its Asia headquarters in Singapore on 26 November, after receiving a Capital Markets Services License from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

The headquarters is led by Jonathan Belz, global chief executive officer, and Tina Gill, managing director, Asia.

BFA has built relationships with leading US venture and growth managers for over two decades, with some dating back to 2005. Its direct investments include SpaceX, Anthropic, OpenAI, Databricks and Anduril, alongside emerging artificial intelligence firms such as Higgsfield, Groq, Decart and Instinct.

Jonathan Belz has over 20 years of experience in investment banking and private markets, working at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse, across Australia, Hong Kong and the US.

Meanwhile, Tina Gill has more than a decade of investment experience in Singapore, most recently as portfolio manager at an institutionalised Singapore-based family office. Prior to that, she worked at Brookfield Asset Management.

Since its establishment in 2019, BFA has grown to six offices across Australia, Asia and the US, with more than $428.5m (AU$500m) in assets under administration as of 1 October.

"Singapore is where Asia's private wealth is being built and managed and our MAS licence means we can now serve investors directly from the region. It’s the foundation for expanding BFA across Asia as we grow our team and our investor relationships here,” said Belz.

AU$1=SG$0.86 as of 26 November.

data.title: Fraud and scam claims rise 18%, remain top financial dispute
data.description:
Most cases involved compromised credentials and unauthorised bank transactions.

The Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre Ltd (FIDReC) received 1,515 fraud and scam claims in the financial year ending 30 June, up 18% year on year from 1,285, making it the largest claim type for the third consecutive year.

The majority of fraud and scam claims involved compromised credentials and unauthorised transactions on customers’ bank accounts, FIDReC said.

Overall claims across all categories rose 23% to a record 5,344, from 4,355 previously.

Claims relating to financial institutions’ practices and policies increased 37% to 889, from 649. Service standards claims recorded the largest increase, rising 61% to 520 from 323, whilst market conduct claims grew 11% to 432 from 389.

Claims also increased across all categories of financial institutions. Banks, finance companies, and credit bureaus accounted for 2,009 claims, compared with 1,831 previously.

Life and composite insurers recorded 481 claims, up from 323, whilst general and composite insurers saw claims rise to 474 from 297. Capital markets services licensees logged 163 claims, up from 94.

Licensed financial advisers and insurance brokers recorded 104 claims, compared with 84 previously. Claims involving payment service providers jumped to 125 from 17.
